original_value: Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR), as an active sensor transmitting long wavelengths, has the advantages of working day and night and without rain or cloud disturbance. It is further able to sense the geometric structure of forests more than passive optical sensors, making it a valuable tool for mapping forest Above Ground Biomass (AGB). This paper studies the ability of the single- and multi-temporal C-band Sentinel-1 and polarimetric L-band PALSAR-2 data to estimate live AGB based on ground truth data collected in New England, USA in 2017. Comparisons of results using the Simple Water Cloud Model (SWCM) on both VH and VV polarizations show that C-band reaches saturation much faster than the L-band due to its limited forest canopy penetration. The exhaustive search multiple linear regression model over the many polarimetric parameters from PALSAR-2 data shows that the combination of polarimetric parameters could slightly improve the AGB estimation, with an adjusted R2 as high as 0.43 and RMSE of around 70 Mg/ha when decomposed Pv component and Alpha angle are used. Additionally, the single- and multi-temporal C-band Sentinel-1 data are compared, which demonstrates that the multi-temporal Sentinel-1 significantly improves the AGB estimation, but still has a much lower adjusted R2 due to the limitations of the short wavelength. Finally, a site-level comparison between paired control and treatment sites shows that the L-band aligns better with the ground truth than the C-band, showing the high potential of the models to be applied to relative biomass change detection.

result.paraphrase: Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR), as an active sensor that transmits long wavelengths, can operate day and night and is unaffected by rain or clouds. It can also detect forest geometric structure better than passive optical sensors, which makes it useful for mapping forest Above Ground Biomass (AGB). This paper evaluates how well single- and multi-temporal C-band Sentinel-1 and polarimetric L-band PALSAR-2 data estimate live AGB using ground-truth data collected in New England, USA, in 2017. Using the Simple Water Cloud Model (SWCM) with both VH and VV polarizations, the results show that C-band saturates much faster than L-band because of its limited penetration of the forest canopy. An exhaustive-search multiple linear regression model over the many polarimetric parameters from PALSAR-2 data indicates that combining polarimetric parameters can slightly improve AGB estimation, with an adjusted R2 up to 0.43 and RMSE of about 70 Mg/ha when the decomposed Pv component and Alpha angle are used. In addition, comparing single- and multi-temporal C-band Sentinel-1 data shows that multi-temporal Sentinel-1 significantly improves AGB estimation, although its adjusted R2 remains much lower because of the short wavelength limitation. Finally, a site-level comparison of paired control and treatment sites finds that L-band matches the ground truth better than C-band, highlighting the strong potential of these models for relative biomass change detection.
